EU-ForDAM: gap-filling test and gap-filled dataset (v1)

PhD objective 1: harmonising incomplete records

Published

October 22, 2026

The question

Most gaps in EU-ForDAM are insects a country never reported. Following the thesis premise, the existing records carry information about the missing ones, we estimate those gaps from the insects that were reported. Rules: 0 = monitored, no damage (kept); not reported = unknown (estimated, never set to 0); host tree absent from the region = 0 (forest table of Hlasny et al. 2025); value1 only; the Czech spruce bark-borer group counted as I. typographus as in the paper.

How methods were tested

Real reported values were hidden in whole country x insect blocks (exactly the shape of a real gap: a country without any record of an insect), predicted from the rest, and compared with the truth: 17,351 hidden cells, 10 rounds. Insects reported by only one country cannot be tested this way.

Method What it does
Simple average the insect’s mean in that year (the yardstick)
Partner method borrows from insects linked to it (correlation metrics) recorded in the same region-year
Factor model latent factor model using all insects at once, in two parts: any damage? x how much?; each insect’s level pulled towards its broad group
+ forest area the factor model plus host-forest area per region (NUTS forest table)

method error per cell (log) damage vs no damage (AUC) totals within 2x typical total error (x off)
simple average 4.00 0.64 8% 45.70
partner method 3.77 0.68 11% 25.17
factor model 3.43 0.76 25% 4.60
factor model + forest area 3.57 0.72 26% 4.54
factor model + forest area (amount only) 3.41 0.76 25% 4.54

Result. Methods that use the other insects beat the simple average, which supports the thesis premise. The factor model is clearly best: it separates damage from no damage much better (AUC 0.76 vs 0.64) and gets regional totals far closer (typically 4.54x off vs 46x), because it learns each region’s overall level from all its other insects. Forest area adds only a little, and only when used for the amounts.

The best method differs by insect; the partner method wins for several conifer bark beetles with strong, consistent partners.

Attempts to improve further

method error per cell (log) damage vs no damage (AUC) totals within 2x typical total error (x off)
factor model (v1) 3.39 0.76 25% 4.54
recalibrated only 3.42 0.74 8% 26.96
+ memory 3.42 0.75 8% 26.63
+ neighbours 3.37 0.74 7% 34.91
+ reporting effect 3.44 0.74 8% 26.21
+ all three 3.39 0.75 7% 31.10
+ all three, Tweedie 5.06 0.73 22% 6.03

Memory (the region’s other insects last year), neighbouring regions (NUTS positions), a country reporting effect and a Tweedie distribution were added as a second stage. None beat the factor model: memory and reporting level are already captured by it through the other insects; neighbours carry a little extra information, but adding them as a second stage disturbs the level and damages totals. This suggests the model is close to what the damage records alone can predict; further gains likely need external drivers (drought/VPD, storms) and spatial structure inside the model.

The gap-filled dataset v2 (factor model only, with ranges)

Changes from v1: the same data as the correlation metrics (Czech spruce bark-borer group counted as I. typographus); the factor model only (no partner method); aggregate reporting codes are not filled; every filled total has an 80% range taken from the hide-and-predict test.

value_type confidence cells share
filled reliable 6083 7%
filled untested 14552 17%
filled weak 14150 17%
not fillable (nothing recorded in this region-year) NA 11898 14%
not filled: aggregate reporting code NA 5943 7%
reported damage NA 9814 12%
reported zero NA 16923 20%
zero: host tree absent NA 5645 7%

Ranges. The final model was re-run 10 times, each time with different country x insect blocks hidden. For every hidden country x insect x year total the real value is known, so the spread of real / predicted tells how far off a filled total typically is; its 10% and 90% points give the 80% range (per insect when it has at least 30 hidden totals). Check: learning the spread on half the folds, 74% of the other half’s real totals fall inside the 80% range (target 80%), so the ranges are slightly too narrow.

Confidence. Reliable = in the test, the model beats the simple average for that insect and separates damage from no damage (AUC >= 0.7): 9 insects (den_pin, dip_sp, lym_dis, neo_ser, pan_fla, pha_cya, pis_pin, pit_spp, pol_pol). Weak = tested but not both: 20 insects. Untested = recorded in one country only; filled but left out of totals.

Caution. For several insects the filled damage is many times the reported damage (e.g. Ips duplicatus, Pissodes pini, Thaumetopoea pityocampa, Lymantria monacha). The model fills every region where the host tree grows and something was recorded, including countries outside an insect’s geographic range (the pine processionary moth is Mediterranean). A country x insect “could occur here” mask (range maps or expert judgement) is needed before Europe-wide totals are used.

The gap-filled dataset v3 (current): better model + draft range rule

Retooled on the 2025 paper’s hierarchy. Aggregate reporting codes (several insects lumped together) are model input only: they help the model learn the region-year patterns but are never filled, and all test scores below are on single insects. The spruce bark-borer group of CZ and DE is counted as I. typographus, and tha_pit is T. pityocampa (filled only in BG, CH, HR, IT, SI), both as in the paper. Totals are reported per paper group, with the aggregates added into the reported part:

Better model (M2). Six versions of the factor model were compared in the same hide-and-predict test. The chosen one (M2) separates each region-year’s overall intensity into region and year parts and uses 3 hidden factors whose insect sensitivities are pulled towards the insect’s broad group.

model error (log) AUC totals within 2x typical total off (x) usable pairs the model links
M0 current 3.37 0.78 25% 4.64 13 of 28
M1 region+year (pull 5) 3.37 0.79 27% 4.48 14 of 28
M1 region+year (pull 20) 3.37 0.78 27% 4.56 16 of 28
M2 K=3 + group links 3.34 0.79 27% 4.35 22 of 28
M2 K=4 + group links 3.34 0.79 27% 4.35 22 of 28
M2 K=4, no group links 3.36 0.79 26% 4.64 13 of 28

M2 is slightly better at filling (AUC 0.78 to 0.79, typical total error 4.64x to 4.35x) and reproduces far more of the usable insect pairs from the correlation metrics (22 of 28 instead of 13). It was picked out of six versions on the same test, so its lead is slightly optimistic.

Draft range rule. An insect is filled only in countries that report damage from it or share a border with one that does; elsewhere the cell is 0 (“outside range”). This is a data-only stand-in for an expert range table (outputs/tables/GF2_range_draft_for_correction.xlsx). tha_pit is Thaumetopoea pityocampa (as in the paper) and is allowed only in BG, CH, HR, IT and SI.

Ranges: 74% of hidden real totals fall inside the 80% range (target 80%). Reliable insects: 15; weak: 14.

With the range rule, for most insects the filled part is 0.1-1x the reported damage. Still implausibly high and needing expert range checks: Pissodes pini (9x reported), Polygraphus poligraphus (7x), Ips duplicatus (3x).

The gap-filled dataset v4: v3 rebuilt on the shared host table

Same model (M2) and range rule as v3. What changed is the host information each insect gets: it is now the same host table used for the host-share, totals and correlation work. For example, L. monacha is “spruce and pine” (all conifers), Melolontha is “all forest”, Zeiraphera is “larch”, and L. dispar and A. viridis are “broadleaves”. Recorded damage on a tree shows that the wider forest column is there too (spruce, pine, fir → conifers; oak → broadleaves).

model error (log) AUC totals within 2x typical total off (x) usable pairs linked
v3 (M2, old host labels) 3.34 0.79 27% 4.35 22 of 28
v4 (M2, shared host table) 3.31 0.80 29% 4.21 22 of 28
group unit reported filled filled vs reported
Borers on angiosperms m3 10,869,383 2,940,245 27%
Borers on gymnosperms m3 686,541,052 36,130,438 5%
Defoliators on angiosperms ha 6,629,198 2,606,910 39%
Defoliators on gymnosperms ha 5,832,112 1,803,938 31%
  • Test scores: slightly better on every measure. This was not tuned on the test, so it is a fair gain.
  • Generalists (L. dispar, Melolontha, Geometridae, …) are no longer set to 0 in the 19 regions without oak.
  • L. monacha: filled damage falls from 2.7 to 0.4 million ha. v3 scaled it by spruce area: Poland has little spruce, so the rate per spruce hectare was huge, and Austria got 1.5 million ha. It is now scaled by all conifers.
  • Check: no filled region-year is above 10% of its host (the highest is 9.5%). Reported values go up to 67%, so the fills are typical years and never outbreaks.
  • Still implausible: Zeiraphera griseana (larch bud moth), with 616,000 ha filled from 958 ha reported, 446,000 ha of it in Poland. Larch has no column in the forest appendix, and scaling by all conifers gives Poland’s pine forests to a larch insect. Also insects reported by only 2–3 countries and filled into AT, CH, PL and SK: S. ratzeburgi, S. scolytus, Neodiprion, Polygraphus, P. pini (9–22x reported).

v4b (current) and v5: hosts without their own forest data

Two ways to stop larch, birch, elm and poplar insects being scaled by a stand-in area (all conifers / all broadleaves):

  • v4b: v4, but these insects get the model’s plain (unscaled) amount.
  • v5: the 2025 paper’s approach. Nothing is scaled; log(host area) is a model input, and the model learns for each insect how strongly damage rises with it.
model error (log) AUC totals within 2x typical total off (x) usable pairs linked
v4 (M2, shared host table) 3.31 0.80 29% 4.21 22 of 28
v4b (no stand-in host areas) 3.31 0.80 29% 4.15 21 of 28
v5 (host area as a model input) 3.35 0.79 18% 8.22 21 of 28
version filled cells highest share of host above 100% of host
v4b 21738 10% 0
v5 21738 2481% 138
  • v4b is kept as the current version. Its scores are the same as v4’s or slightly better, and no filled value is above 10.1% of its host. Zeiraphera falls from 616,000 to 155,000 ha filled; S. ratzeburgi and S. scolytus fall by a third.
  • v5 fails as a gap-filler. Totals are typically 8x off, and 138 filled cells are above 100% of their host. The learned slopes go up to 2.9 (damage rising much faster than host), and they extrapolate badly to regions with very large host areas. The paper used host area to explain differences between regions in a trend model. It was never used to predict new regions, and that is where it breaks.
  • Still to fix: most of Zeiraphera’s remaining fill is in Poland (128,000 ha), and Dendroctonus micans’s fill is 1.7 million m³ from 3,500 m³ reported. Both are “weak” insects; D. micans is filled worse than a simple average. They come from the draft range rule and from weak fills being counted in the totals.

How to read it

  • Reported values are untouched; every filled value carries its method and confidence.
  • Filled values are good for whether and when damage occurred, rough for how much (a single regional total is typically several times off).
  • Europe-wide totals: use reported + reliable fills; treat weak and untested fills as indications only.
